episode.throughLine: Unemployment payments gave her time to write while she feared that her relatives were right about a steadier job. She tried to rework a novel when a minor character grew central; one submitted novel was accepted, another refused, and publication followed in 1976.

contentProfile.contentNote: Includes job loss, financial uncertainty and publication refusals; no death, self-harm or graphic material.

facts.statement: Butler recalled crying at her layoff.

sourceRefs.locator: Paragraph about the final job loss immediately before the account of assembling Patternmaster; Butler's first-person statement, not the reporter's reconstruction.

facts.statement: Octavia E. Butler recalled being twenty-seven, laid off, supported by unemployment compensation and afraid that her writing would never succeed.

sourceRefs.locator: Final answer, paragraph beginning 'I was able to find the time'.

facts.statement: Butler said the idea for Patternmaster came when she was twelve, but she did not yet know how to write a novel and tried for years before she could write it.

sourceRefs.locator: Answer to 'Where do you get your ideas?'

facts.statement: Butler recalled rising at two or three in the morning to write before office, factory or warehouse work; she disliked the jobs, left jobs and found others, and accumulated rejections.
Butler recalled throwing away all her accumulated rejection slips one day in disgust.
At eighteen Butler won a college writing contest and received fifteen dollars, her first money from writing; at twenty-three she sold two short stories to writers teaching at Clarion.
Butler said only one of those two stories was published, and she sold no other writing for five years before selling her first novel.
Butler feared that relatives urging a civil-service job might be right; she remembered feeling desperate during the period of unemployment-supported novel writing.

In the Beal interview, Butler described writing Mind of My Mind while Patternmaster was with a publisher, then submitting it elsewhere. In the earlier Bogstad interview she said Mind of My Mind was finished first. The candidate does not resolve the accounts into a single composition order.

sourceRefs.locator: Final answer, paragraph beginning 'I had my first short stories'.

Printed p. 31 left column, paragraph after the lost-manuscript account, ending with the statement that Patternmaster needed less work. Comparison concerns completion order only, not the order of publisher replies.

facts.statement: Butler recalled trying to reorganize Patternmaster at about the halfway point because Amber, intended as a minor character, had become central.

sourceRefs.locator: Printed p. 30 right column, final answer, continuing through p. 31 left column, first two answers. The paragraph before the Mind of My Mind question gives an approximate midpoint and attempted reorganization, then explicitly expresses hope rather than certainty that it succeeded.

facts.statement: Butler said the idea for Mind of My Mind came when she was fifteen and the idea for Survivor when she was nineteen.

sourceRefs.locator: Answer to 'Where do you get your ideas?'

facts.statement: While those two novels were under consideration, Butler began revising Survivor, an old novel begun in her teens.
While working on Survivor, Butler received a rejection of Mind of My Mind and an acceptance of Patternmaster; she did not specify the delivery medium, day, order or her physical reaction.

sourceRefs.locator: Final answer, paragraph beginning 'And while I was working on Survivor'.

facts.statement: Butler said she sold Patternmaster in 1975 and it was published in 1976.
Butler said her first novel's publication in 1976 enabled her first vacation: a month-long bus pass trip that included New York, Seattle and national parks.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening answers, beginning 'I went to Seattle for the first time in 1976'.

facts.statement: Butler remembered that on the trip she and a woman with uncomfortable shoes encouraged each other up the Empire State Building and reached the top. Butler said she herself was out of shape; the other woman's difficulty was her feet.

sourceRefs.locator: Answer to 'What'd you think of New York?'

facts.statement: Octavia E. Butler was a science-fiction novelist and the author of Patternmaster.

arc.canonicalText:
She was twenty-seven when she lost her job. She cried.

Before the layoff, she had fitted writing around paid work. She got up in the early morning to write, then left for the office, factory or warehouse. She left jobs she hated and found others.

She had sold two stories years earlier. Only one had appeared. Nothing else had sold since.
arc.sourceNote: Refinement 2026-09-09. The opening now starts with a reported event rather than a manuscript retrospective. Fact-016 is the only new claim from Warrick. The next paragraphs explicitly step back; workday routine and early story outcomes are not staged on the layoff day. No room, notice, time of day, cause of dismissal or invented gesture. A situated single-location scene remains unavailable; craft HOLD stays. September 10 rewrite note: this beat is unchanged; prior scene, scope and length holds are not cleared by the new manuscript-revision evidence.

arc.canonicalText:
Unemployment payments were supporting her while she wrote. She was afraid that nothing would come of the writing.

Her relatives thought she should get a steady government job. She feared they might be right.

She had been trying to write a novel from an idea she first had at twelve. Having an idea had come long before knowing how to make a book. She was working, and still afraid.
arc.sourceNote: Refinement 2026-09-09. Removed abstract padding about where fear belonged and the repeated sales recap. Interiority is Butler's retrospective testimony, probable in the record. This remains a period-level fear; it is not claimed to be her thoughts at the instant of the layoff. No invented family conversation or private decision. September 10 rewrite note: this beat is unchanged; prior scene, scope and length holds are not cleared by the new manuscript-revision evidence.

arc.canonicalText:
A woman in the novel was meant to have only a small part. But her role kept growing as the book went on.

About halfway through, the writer could no longer leave that character as she was. She went back and tried to reorganize the story. She wanted the woman to seem to have belonged there from the beginning.

Her first plan had changed.
arc.sourceNote: Source-grounded rewrite 2026-09-10. A specific manuscript intervention replaces the former multi-novel period summary. Butler's own retrospective explanation, not an invented writing gesture. No desk, room, exact day or elapsed revision time is claimed. The writing-stage response is better bounded but the source does not date this intervention within 1974–1975; episode-fit and R2 review remain held. Independent-C correction: approximate halfway point and attempted revision are preserved; the interview does not assert that the structural change succeeded. Chronology HOLD: placement after the layoff passage must not be read as evidence that this undated revision occurred after the layoff. That sequence is not established by Janus.

arc.canonicalText:
Two of her novels went to different publishers. While both were under consideration, she began revising an older book. She had started that one in her teens.

Her writing had earned money before. At eighteen, she had won money in a college contest. Later, two writers teaching a workshop bought stories from her. Only one appeared.

Five years followed without another sale. She was revising again.
arc.sourceNote: Source-grounded rewrite 2026-09-10. The two-submission/third-revision state is retained without claiming which novel was first completed. Bogstad p. 31 and Beal's final answer do not support a confidently unified completion sequence. College and short-story earnings remain explicit safeguards against the first-money myth. Compression belongs in this beat; the outcomes follow without an invented order.

arc.canonicalText:
During those revisions, her two submissions received different answers. One was accepted; the other was refused.

The accepted novel was the one in which the woman's role had grown. The other manuscript was still without a publisher.

One book was going into print.
arc.sourceNote: Source-grounded rewrite 2026-09-10. Removed 'first manuscript' and 'second manuscript' labels, which over-neatly ordered works in light of the newly read Bogstad interview. Outcomes remain explicitly unordered within Survivor revision. The novel is linked to the documented revision, not to an invented acceptance scene. No letter, phone call, day, room or reaction is supplied. The turn's R2 scene hold remains. Independent-C correction: callback identifies the growing character, not a proven successful reorganization.

arc.canonicalText:
The book came out the next year. After it was published, she took her first vacation. She bought a bus pass that let her travel for a month. She went to cities she had not visited before.

In one city, she met another woman who was sightseeing. They climbed a tall building together. The woman's shoes hurt. The writer was out of shape. They encouraged each other on the way up. She remembered that they made it to the top.

For once, the time away from a job was a holiday. There was a month to travel.
arc.sourceNote: Research continuation 2026-09-05; cross-review correction 2026-09-05. Bounded 1976 coda from Butler's own 2004 recollection. The writer is Butler, who described herself as out of shape; her companion's difficulty was uncomfortable shoes. Identity stays stable but metadata extends beyond the 1974–1975 stage label. No ascent-as-success advice; no claim that first publication ended money worries. September 10 rewrite note: this beat is unchanged; prior scene, scope and length holds are not cleared by the new manuscript-revision evidence.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Octavia Butler.

She wrote science-fiction novels.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You can care about something without feeling certain it will work. You can still be unsure.
arc.sourceNote: Research continuation 2026-09-05. Fixed distance then non-directive permission; no promise that persistence earns publication. September 10 rewrite note: this beat is unchanged; prior scene, scope and length holds are not cleared by the new manuscript-revision evidence.

dramatizationLimits: No invented delivery medium, response gesture, work room, dated rejection encounter or private dialogue.
Keep recollections probable and openly framed; no diary or manuscript claimed opened.
The unemployment-supported period is not a reconstruction of a single day. No motivational notebook inscription is relocated into it.
The Bogstad interview supplies a specific manuscript intervention but not its date or writing location. Do not attach the undated lost-briefcase episode to age twenty-seven.
The Patternmaster revision was an attempt at about the halfway point; do not harden approximate timing or claim that her structural aim certainly succeeded.
avoidRules: Do not say first novel advance was her first writing money.
Do not call Patternmaster the third novel written in the unemployed period.
Do not equate a refusal with racism when its reason is unrecorded.
No career award list or advice to quit paid work.
Do not conflate selling short stories in 1970 with publication dates.
Do not call Patternmaster the first novel she finished. The Bogstad and Beal accounts must not be silently forced into one completion chronology.

sources.citation: Butler, Octavia E., interviewed by Joshunda Sanders. Interview first published Africana.com, February 24, 2004; In Motion Magazine, March 14, 2004; republished by interviewer on Medium.

sources.locator: Job-loss paragraph directly before Patternmaster's synopsis. Consulted for fact-016 only; no room, notification method or acceptance scene taken from this account.

sources.citation: Octavia E. Butler interviewed by Janice Bogstad at IguanaCon, transcribed by Toni Petriunas. Janus 14, vol. 4 no. 4, Winter 1978/79, pp. 29–31. Original issue preserved by SF3.
sources.locator: Printed pp. 29–31 (PDF indices 29–31), visually read 2026-09-10. The Patternmaster revision account crosses pp. 30–31. Later on p. 31 Butler says Mind of My Mind was finished first; this conflicts with a simple reading of the Beal interview's composition sequence. Neither the revision day nor its exact location is given.
